newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bad news for Irish govt in pre-election poll.
newsitem.headline: Bad news for Irish govt in pre-election poll.

text.p: The Irish government was dealt a pre-election blow on Wednesday when an opinion poll showed that a key coalition partner, the Labour party, has lost almost half its support in Dublin

The poll, in the Evening Herald newspaper, was published amid renewed speculation that Prime Minister John Bruton will call an election on May 23, six months early, to capitalise on a booming economy and rising employment.
But, according to the poll, his Labour coalition partner could lose up to six seats in Dublin, where around one third of the country's parliamentary seats are located.
It also showed that the opposition Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrat parties were gaining support ahead of elections in which drugs, crime and unemployment are expected to be the main issues.
The poll showed that Labour's support in the capital has fallen from 26 percent in 1992 elections to 14 percent this month and that Labour's share of parliamentary seats could drop from 32 to 26.
This would be a severe blow to Bruton's chances of rebuilding the coalition of his Fine Gael party, which has 47 seats, Labour and the small Democratic Left, which has six.
Political analysts believe Dublin holds the key to victory in the election, which has to be held by November this year but is expected much sooner.
Speculation on an early poll intensified when Minister of State Joan Burton, of the Labour party, let slip that "there is actually about five weeks to run to this election."
Bruton's government has declined to be drawn on such speculation but political sources say it could call the election on May 1 with a three-week campaign period.
This would allow Ireland to take a full part in crucial European Union meetings on a single currency and enlargement which are expected in June.
Ireland is an enthusiastic candidate for Economic and Monetary Union and is also keen to safeguard its own interests and those of other small states in any revisions of the bloc's founding treaties.
Bruton's government came to power in November 1994 when Labour withdrew its support from the government of Prime Minister Albert Reynolds of Fianna Fail in a row over legal appointments.
Opinion polls show that Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats hold a six-point lead over Bruton's coalition but that the gap is narrowing.
